## About the Series

*The 100* is an American post-apocalyptic science fiction drama developed by *Jason Rothenberg*. The show is loosely based on the novel series written by *Kass Morgan*.

The story begins ninety-seven years after a devastating nuclear apocalypse wiped out almost all life on Earth. The only known survivors lived on a massive space station known as the 'Ark'. Facing failing life-support systems, the Ark's leaders send 100 juvenile delinquents down to the surface to determine if Earth has become habitable again.

As these teens, including *Clarke Griffin*, *Bellamy Blake*, *Octavia Blake*, and *Raven Reyes*, struggle to survive the harsh conditions of the ground, they soon discover they are not alone. They must navigate complex relationships and moral dilemmas while encountering groups such as the *Grounders*, *Mountain Men*, and various factions vying for survival in a reclaimed world.

Over the course of seven seasons, *The 100* explores themes of survival, sacrifice, and the lengths humanity will go to in order to ensure its future.

# Viewership Statistics

The series debuted on March 19, 2014, with a strong pilot episode that garnered **2.73 million** viewers. Over its seven-season run, the show transitioned from a high-stakes survival drama to a complex exploration of tribalism, technology, and morality.

```{r season_summary, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
season_data <- data.frame(
  Season = 1:7,
  Episodes = c(13, 16, 16, 13, 13, 13, 16),
  First_Released = c("March 19, 2014", "October 22, 2014", "January 21, 2016", 
                     "February 1, 2017", "April 24, 2018", "April 30, 2019", "May 20, 2020"),
  Last_Released = c("June 11, 2014", "March 11, 2015", "May 19, 2016", 
                    "May 24, 2017", "August 7, 2018", "August 6, 2019", "September 30, 2020"),
  Rank = c(150, 157, 165, 158, 182, 165, 179),
  Avg_Viewers_Millions = c(2.59, 2.46, 1.94, 1.47, 1.61, 1.30, 1.06)
)

kable(season_data, 
      col.names = c("Season", "Episodes", "First Released", "Last Released", "Rank", "Avg Viewers (Millions)"),
      align = "cccccc")
```

# Viewership Over Time
```{r average_bar_chart, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
viewers <- c(2.73, 2.27, 1.90, 1.69, 1.80, 1.97, 1.88, 1.64, 1.73, 1.46, 1.71, 1.58, 1.68,
             1.54, 1.48, 1.68, 1.75, 1.64, 1.86, 1.62, 1.40, 1.48, 1.53, 1.51, 1.36, 1.42, 1.55, 1.49, 1.34,
             1.88, 1.63, 1.57, 1.32, 1.36, 1.41, 1.39, 1.20, 1.23, 1.13, 1.08, 1.15, 1.27, 1.13, 1.17, 1.29,
             1.21, 1.01, 1.05, 1.00, 1.02, 0.98, 0.90, 0.97, 0.81, 0.85, 0.86, 0.83, 0.91,
             1.43, 1.02, 1.08, 1.07, 0.94, 0.92, 0.83, 0.73, 0.89, 0.86, 0.85, 0.88, 0.99,
             0.86, 0.81, 0.82, 0.73, 0.73, 0.64, 0.72, 0.63, 0.70, 0.57, 0.54, 0.61, 0.59,
             0.80, 0.76, 0.71, 0.63, 0.68, 0.57, 0.64, 0.67, 0.61, 0.47, 0.58, 0.54, 0.59, 0.63, 0.52, 0.61)

seasons <- c(rep("1", 13), rep("2", 16), rep("3", 16), rep("4", 13), rep("5", 13), rep("6", 13), rep("7", 16))
df <- data.frame(Episode = 1:100, Viewers = viewers, Season = seasons)

# Averages
seasonal_avg <- df %>%
  group_by(Season) %>%
  summarise(MeanViewers = mean(Viewers))

# Bar plot
ggplot(seasonal_avg, aes(x = Season, y = MeanViewers, fill = Season)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", color = "white", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(MeanViewers, 2)), vjust = -0.5, size = 4) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(title = "Average Viewership per Season",
       y = "Average Viewers (Millions)", x = "Season") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  ylim(0, 2.2)
```

```{r viewership_trend, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Line chart
ggplot(df, aes(x = Episode, y = Viewers, color = Season)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(title = "The 100: U.S. Viewership Trend (100 Episodes)",
       y = "Viewers (Millions)", x = "Episode Number") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The graph above tracks the U.S. viewership (in millions) for every episode of the series. While there is a clear downward trend common in long-running cable dramas, the show maintained a dedicated cult following.

The series peaked with the **Pilot (`r viewers[1]` million)** and concluded with **`r viewers[length(viewers)]` million**. However, the curve flattens significantly after Season 4, indicating that while the show lost casual viewers, it successfully retained a loyal core audience.

```{r season_boxplot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Boxplot
ggplot(df, aes(x = Season, y = Viewers, fill = Season)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8, outlier.color = "red") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(title = "Viewership Distribution per Season",
       y = "Viewers (Millions)", x = "Season") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The **Boxplot** provides insights into audience reliability:

 * **Seasons 1-3:** High medians and high variance suggest a show finding its footing.

 * **Seasons 4-5:** A "correction" period with smaller variance, reflecting critical reception.

 * **Seasons 6-7:** Small "boxes" suggest a stabilized niche audience. Fans who watched these seasons were highly dedicated and unlikely to drop the series before the end.

# Ratings over episodes
```{r episode_rankings, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Constructing a matrix of ratings (Seasons x Episodes)
# NA values represent non-existent episodes (shorter seasons)

# AI (Gemini 3) was used to rewrite data from source file to structured matrix format for plotting
ratings_vals <- matrix(c(
  7.3, 7.3, 7.7, 7.7, 8.0, 7.8, 8.0, 7.7, 8.1, 8.1, 7.8, 8.3, 8.8, NA, NA, NA,
  8.2, 8.1, 8.1, 8.1, 8.3, 8.2, 8.4, 8.8, 8.1, 8.1, 8.6, 8.4, 8.5, 8.6, 8.7, 9.2,
  7.7, 8.1, 8.6, 8.4, 7.8, 8.0, 6.9, 7.0, 7.1, 7.2, 7.6, 7.2, 7.6, 7.5, 7.7, 7.9,
  7.6, 7.6, 7.8, 7.9, 8.1, 7.7, 7.7, 7.9, 7.9, 9.1, 8.1, 8.6, 9.1, NA, NA, NA,
  8.5, 8.6, 8.8, 8.4, 8.0, 8.0, 8.0, 8.3, 8.4, 8.0, 8.2, 8.7, 9.5, NA, NA, NA,
  8.3, 8.3, 8.1, 8.3, 8.5, 8.0, 8.2, 8.0, 8.1, 8.2, 8.1, 8.5, 8.0, NA, NA, NA,
  7.5, 8.0, 7.3, 7.8, 8.3, 7.5, 7.4, 9.0, 7.7, 8.0, 7.5, 7.5, 4.8, 6.1, 6.4, 6.7 
), nrow = 7, byrow = TRUE)

colnames(ratings_vals) <- paste0("E", 1:16)
rownames(ratings_vals) <- paste0("S", 1:7)

# Transform the matrix into a long-format data frame
rankings_df <- as.data.frame(ratings_vals) %>%
  mutate(Season = rownames(ratings_vals)) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("E"), names_to = "Episode", values_to = "Rating") %>%
  filter(!is.na(Rating)) %>%
  # Create the S**E** format column
  mutate(
    Episode_ID = paste0(
      # Ensure Season is S01, S02 etc.
      gsub("S", "S0", Season), 
      # Ensure Episode is E01, E02 etc.
      gsub("E", "E", sprintf("E%02d", as.numeric(gsub("E", "", Episode))))
    )
  ) %>%
  select(Episode_ID, Rating)

# Get Top 5 and Bottom 5
top_5 <- rankings_df %>% arrange(desc(Rating)) %>% head(5)
bottom_5 <- rankings_df %>% arrange(Rating) %>% head(5)

# Combine into one table with an empty separator column
# AI (Gemini 3) was used to combine tables
combined_table <- data.frame(
  Top_Episode = top_5$Episode_ID,
  Top_Rating = top_5$Rating,
  Empty_Space = "",
  Bottom_Episode = bottom_5$Episode_ID,
  Bottom_Rating = bottom_5$Rating
)

# 4. Display the combined table
kable(combined_table, 
      col.names = c("Episode", "IMDb Rating", " ", "Episode", "IMDb Rating"), 
      align = "lcclc") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = F) %>%
  add_header_above(c("Top Rated" = 2, " " = 1, "Bottom Rated" = 2)) %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "3em")
```

```{r ratings_heatmap, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
# Reshape data to long format for ggplot2
heatmap_df <- as.data.frame(ratings_vals) %>%
  mutate(Season = rownames(ratings_vals)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("E"), names_to = "Episode", values_to = "Rating")

# Factorize levels to ensure correct plotting order
heatmap_df$Episode <- factor(heatmap_df$Episode, levels = paste0("E", 1:16))
heatmap_df$Season <- factor(heatmap_df$Season, levels = rev(paste0("S", 1:7)))

# Create the heatmap using the gradient color scale
ggplot(heatmap_df, aes(x = Episode, y = Season, fill = Rating)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient(
  low = "#5C4033", high = "#FFD700",  na.value = "white",
  name = "Rating"
) +
  # Add rating value labels inside the tiles
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", Rating)), color = "white", size = 3.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Episode Ratings Heatmap",
       subtitle = "Critical reception across the series (IMDb scores)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

The heatmap above visualizes the critical reception of each episode across all seasons, based on IMDb ratings. The color gradient from dark brown (lower ratings) to gold (higher ratings) allows for quick identification of standout episodes and trends in quality throughout the series. Notably, Season 5 contains some of the highest-rated episodes, while Season 7 shows a significant drop in ratings, particularly towards the end.

The visualization highlights the show’s "Finale Strength," with standout episodes such as **`r top_5$Episode_ID[1]`** and **`r top_5$Episode_ID[2]`** receiving universal acclaim. In fact, the series reached its critical peak with a rating of **`r top_5$Rating[1]`**. 

Conversely, it captures the controversy of the final season, specifically **`r bottom_5$Episode_ID[1]`**, which represents the lowest point in series reception with a rating of **`r bottom_5$Rating[1]`**. This demonstrates a significant disparity between the show's creative heights and its most divisive moments, as seen in the gap of **`r top_5$Rating[1] - bottom_5$Rating[1]`** points between the best and worst rated episodes.
